raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 64 million people worldwide and carrying substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device-based treatments such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients with symptomatic HF continue to experience limiting symptoms and recurrent hospitalizations [2]. Notably, CRT is only indicated in patients with a prolonged QRS duration, leaving the majority of HF patients with narrow QRS complexes without an electrical device option [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a device-based therapy designed to address this gap, particularly in patients with reduced ejection fraction and narrow QRS [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM therapy delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because these high-voltage signals (approximately 7.5 V) are timed to coincide with the refractory period, they do not initiate a new action potential but instead modulate myocardial contractility [6]. The proposed mechanisms involve enhanced calcium handling, with upregulation of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA2a) and improved phosphorylation of phospholamban, leading to augmented contractile force [7]. Experimental studies have demonstrated reversal of the fetal gene program and normalization of key calcium-cycling proteins following chronic CCM stimulation [8]. These molecular changes suggest that CCM may favorably influence pathological remodeling in addition to providing acute inotropic support without increasing myocardial oxygen demand to the degree seen with pharmacologic inotropes [9].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has been supported by several randomized controlled trials. The FIX-HF-5 study evaluated CCM in patients with NYHA class III–IV HF and ejection fraction ≤35% and found improvements in exercise tolerance measured by peak oxygen consumption and quality of life, although the primary endpoint based on anaerobic threshold was not met across the entire cohort [10]. A prespecified subgroup analysis suggested greater benefit in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [11]. This observation informed the design of the subsequent FIX-HF-5C trial, which enrolled patients with ejection fraction 25–45% and demonstrated significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores [12]. A Bayesian analysis of FIX-HF-5C also indicated a reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization [13].

Earlier feasibility and randomized crossover studies, including the European FIX-CHF-4 trial, established short-term safety and consistent improvements in symptoms and exercise capacity [14]. Pooled and individual patient-level meta-analyses of randomized CCM trials have confirmed improvements in peak VO2 and quality of life, with a favorable safety profile [15]. Long-term registry and observational data have suggested durability of symptomatic benefit and possible reductions in HF hospitalization over multi-year follow-up [16]. The CCM-REG registry reported sustained improvements in NYHA class and quality of life, with mortality rates lower than predicted by the Seattle Heart Failure Model, particularly in patients with ejection fraction 35–45% [17].

## Expanding Indications and Special Populations

There is growing interest in CCM for patients with HF with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, a population with few effective device options [18]. The AbbioCardiac and ongoing trials are exploring CCM in this setting, with preliminary data suggesting symptomatic benefit [19]. CCM has also been studied in patients with atrial fibrillation, where adaptations in signal delivery algorithms are required, and in patients with concomitant CRT or implantable cardioverter-defibrillators [20]. Combination with defibrillator therapy is feasible, although attention to device-device interactions and appropriate sensing is essential [21].

## Safety and Practical Considerations

CCM is delivered via an implantable pulse generator connected to right ventricular leads, with a procedure analogous to pacemaker implantation [22]. The therapy has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with complication rates comparable to other cardiac implantable devices [23]. Battery longevity and the need for daily charging in some systems remain practical considerations, although newer rechargeable-free designs have improved usability [24]. Patient selection remains central, and current guidelines and expert consensus statements recommend CCM for symptomatic HF patients on optimal GDMT who are not candidates for CRT [25].

## Future Directions

Ongoing research aims to clarify the effect of CCM on hard outcomes such as mortality and hospitalization through adequately powered randomized trials [26]. Biomarker and imaging studies are investigating reverse remodeling associated with CCM therapy [27]. Integration of remote monitoring and refinements in signal delivery may further optimize outcomes [28]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that CCM may be economically viable in appropriately selected patients [29]. As the evidence base matures, CCM is increasingly positioned as a valuable adjunct in the device armamentarium for HF [30].
